summary: AI and chip stocks plunge after voters turn on data centres, oil rebounds on new Hormuz attacks, Israel waits for Herzog, Ukraine heads to talks, and a record-warm October.

topics.heading: AI and chip stocks plunge worldwide as voters turn against data centres
topics.summary: US stocks had one of their worst days in years on Thursday, led by a 12% fall in chipmakers, and Asian markets fell further on Friday.[^1][^2] Investors fear the new Democratic Congress and local voters will slow the building of AI data centres.[^4]

lead.title: Global stock rout deepens as AI data centre fears fuel worst US chip sell-off since 2020

alsoReported.title: Stocks plunge as Dem midterm sweep fuels AI regulatory concerns
Why Democrats' win in US midterms could spell trouble for the AI boom

article: On Thursday the S&P 500, an index of 500 large US companies, fell 4.36% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52%, its worst day since April 2025[^2]. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks chipmakers, fell about 12%; Nvidia lost about 9% and memory-chip makers such as Micron fell about 17%[^2][^3]. Euronews reports S&P 500 companies lost a record $2.9 trillion in value in one day[^1]. On Friday Japan's Nikkei fell about 6% and South Korea briefly halted trading after a drop of almost 9%[^6][^1].

The trigger was Tuesday's midterm elections. Electricity prices became a campaign issue, and data centres, the huge buildings full of computers that train and run AI, were on the ballot in at least 40 places; voters backed almost every proposal to halt or restrict them, according to a Guardian count cited by Business Standard[^4]. In Ohio, all 13 town bans on the ballot looked set to pass in early results[^5]. Senator Bernie Sanders called for a national pause on new data centres, and Texas's governor-elect said she would stop approvals until residents are protected[^4].

Why it matters: for two years, much of the stock market's rise has rested on companies spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI buildings and chips. If voters and lawmakers slow that building, the expected profits shrink. One fund manager told Reuters it "feels like the capitulation phase", meaning investors giving up, for those stocks[^2].

My read: a one-day fall, even a record one, does not tell us the AI boom is over. Laws take time, and a Democratic Congress cannot override a veto without Republican votes. But the vote showed something new: AI's physical costs, such as power and land, have become a local political issue. Watch Nvidia's results on November 17 and whether the selling continues next week.
topics.differences: Outlets measure the loss differently: Euronews says S&P 500 companies lost a record $2.9 trillion, while a Reuters column calls the chip index fall its second-biggest on record and Euronews calls it the biggest since 2020[^1][^3]. President Trump blamed the Democrats' win; analysts also point to higher borrowing costs and the Iran war[^1][^2].

topics.heading: Iran says more tankers hit near Hormuz; oil rebounds as Trump weighs his next step
topics.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three more tankers were damaged near the Strait of Hormuz, and Brent crude rose 3.9% to $98.29.[^7][^8] Iran told Russia it will not reopen the strait or negotiate until its conditions are met, while Qatar keeps mediating.[^10]

lead.title: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote

alsoReported.title: Iran's security chief meets Putin, delivers message from Khamenei
Iran's top diplomat speaks with Gulf leaders about tensions, and other Mideast news

article: Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said three more tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, two by sea mines and one by fire; the ships were not named and the claim has not been independently confirmed[^7][^9]. The UK's maritime security agency logged at least five incidents since Sunday and says 35 ships were hit in October, the most in any month of the war, which began on February 28[^7].

Oil reacted fast. A day after Brent crude, the global benchmark, fell more than 8% on hopes of a deal, it rose $3.67, or 3.9%, to settle at $98.29 a barrel[^8]. The consulting firm Eurasia Group now gives a 60% chance of renewed US strikes, 10% for a deal and 30% for a continued standoff, and says escalation could push Brent to $110 to $125[^8].

In Moscow, Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei handed President Putin a letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Rezaei said Iran "will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations" with the US until its seven conditions are met; Putin said Russia is ready to help end the war[^10]. Iran's foreign minister also called Gulf neighbours, and Qatar's statement stressed freedom of navigation[^9][^10].

In Washington, Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war for the midterm defeat[^7]. Trump said late Thursday he would soon decide whether to widen the war, saying the US might have to "destroy the rest of the country" though he would rather not[^11]. Two Reuters sources think new strikes are still likely[^7]. Qatar's draft plan for three days of confidence-building steps has no meeting date yet[^11]. My read: both sides are testing whether the US vote changed the other's position, and the strait stays dangerous meanwhile.
topics.differences: Accounts of Thursday's incidents differ: Reuters reports the IRGC saying two ships hit mines and one caught fire, while AP reports Iranian state TV saying two tankers and a towboat caught fire; AP could not verify it[^7][^9]. Iran says it needs the US blockade and sanctions lifted first; a senior Iranian official says the sides remain far apart[^7][^11].

topics.heading: Eisenkot wins 67 recommendations; Herzog will name Israel's next PM candidate Sunday
topics.summary: Parties with 67 of the Knesset's 120 seats recommended Gadi Eisenkot as prime minister, against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu.[^12] President Herzog will decide on Sunday who gets the first chance to form a government.[^12][^13]

lead.title: As Eisenkot wins 67 nods to be PM, Herzog says he'll announce mandate decision on Sunday

alsoReported.title: Eisenkot leads Netanyahu 67-46, but Herzog delays mandate decision until Sunday
Four people, including a child, killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza

article: After Israel's election, the president meets every party and asks whom they recommend as prime minister, then gives one person the first chance, called the mandate, to build a coalition with a majority of the Knesset, Israel's 120-seat parliament. Those talks ended on Thursday: parties with 67 seats backed Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who leads the Yashar party, and parties with 46 backed Netanyahu[^12].

Eisenkot's backers include centre and left parties, Avigdor Liberman's right-wing Yisrael Beytenu, and two Arab-led parties, Ra'am and the Joint List[^13]. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (7 seats) recommended no one, a blow to Netanyahu, who has relied on it[^12][^13]. Herzog called the result "clear" but said he must judge whether a government can actually be formed, and will announce his choice on Sunday, November 8[^12][^13]. The new Knesset is sworn in on November 10[^12].

A recommendation is not a coalition. A Times of Israel analysis says only 48 of the 67 are firm allies: Liberman rules out relying on Arab parties, and UTJ's demand to keep army-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men clashes with Eisenkot's camp[^15]. Netanyahu's Likud warns against a government that depends on Arab parties[^13].

In Gaza, where a ceasefire has held unevenly since October 2025, Al Jazeera reports at least four people killed in Israeli strikes on Thursday. Gaza's Health Ministry, run by Hamas, says 1,602 people have been killed since the ceasefire began[^14]. My read: who leads Israel's next government will shape the next phase of the Gaza plan, so Sunday's decision matters well beyond Israel.
topics.differences: Likud argues a government relying on Arab-led parties would be illegitimate; Eisenkot's camp says 67 recommendations is the clearest result since 2015 and rules out a unity government with Netanyahu[^12][^13].

topics.heading: Ukraine and partners meet in Brussels as three-way talks with Russia near
topics.summary: Ukraine, the US and European partners met at NATO headquarters on reconstruction and security guarantees, ahead of US-Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.[^16][^17] Strikes continued on both sides, and Kyiv's water was disrupted again.[^18]

lead.title: Russia and Ukraine trade airstrikes as reconstruction and security talks resume in Brussels

alsoReported.title: Ukraine war latest: Kyiv water supply disrupted after power fluctuations due to Russian attacks
Zelensky Holds 90-Minute Discussion With US Envoys Witkoff, Kushner

article: On November 4-5, Ukraine met the US, UK, France, Germany, the EU and NATO in Brussels to discuss rebuilding the country, funding for 2027 and security guarantees, meaning promises from other countries to help defend Ukraine if Russia attacks again; the World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock also took part[^16]. President Zelensky said talks "must move forward at full throttle"[^16].

The next step is Abu Dhabi on November 10-11: the first three-way US-Ukraine-Russia talks since February. US envoy Steve Witkoff says the agenda covers post-war security, de-escalation, humanitarian issues and next steps[^17].

The war goes on meanwhile. Ukraine says it stopped 105 of 128 Russian drones overnight into Thursday, and Russia says it downed 496 Ukrainian drones, many aimed at the Ryazan region, where a refinery fire was reported[^16]. On Friday morning drones reportedly targeted the Afipsky refinery in southern Russia, which Kyiv Post could not confirm[^19]. Kyiv's water supply was disrupted again on Thursday by power problems after Russia's largest attack on energy sites this year[^18].

The toll from Monday's guided-bomb strike on an aid point in Komyshuvakha keeps rising: Zelensky says 43 dead and 33 missing; police told AP 42 bodies have been recovered[^18][^16]. Zelensky also says Ukraine received only 24 US Patriot interceptors in 90 days against a need of about 350 a month[^17]. My read: winter strikes on energy will shape both sides' leverage in Abu Dhabi.
topics.differences: Zelensky says 43 people were killed at Komyshuvakha and 33 are missing; AP, citing police, reports 42 bodies recovered and more than 30 believed trapped[^18][^16]. Drone counts come from each side's military and are not independently checked.

topics.heading: Bank of England raises rates for the first time since 2023, citing war-driven energy costs
topics.summary: The Bank of England raised its key rate from 3.75% to 4% and warned UK inflation could reach about 5% by mid-2027 because of energy costs from the Iran war.[^20] It joins the US Fed and European Central Bank in raising rates.[^20]

lead.title: Bank of England raises key interest rate for first time in over 3 years

article: On Thursday the Bank of England, the UK's central bank, raised its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since August 2023. Eight of its nine policymakers voted for the rise and one wanted a bigger one[^20].

The reason is energy. The bank warned that inflation, the pace at which prices rise, could reach about 5% by mid-2027, up from 3.5% in September, because the Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up oil and gas prices[^20]. Central banks raise rates to cool spending and stop higher prices spreading through the economy, but that also makes mortgages and loans more expensive.

Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes"[^20]. The bank also raised its growth forecast for 2026 to 1.6%[^20]. The move follows recent rate rises by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank[^20]; in the US, traders had seen a 67% chance of another Fed hike in December before Thursday's market fall[^24].

Why it matters: a few years ago, central banks were cutting rates. Now several are raising them again because of a war far away. My read: this shows how one conflict, through the price of oil, reaches household budgets in Britain, Canada and elsewhere.

topics.heading: October was the warmest on record as COP31 climate talks prepare to open in Antalya
topics.summary: Europe's Copernicus climate service says October was the warmest on record, 1.75C above pre-industrial levels, and 2026 is likely the second-hottest year.[^21] UN climate talks open in Antalya, Turkey, on Monday.[^23]

lead.title: 2026 'most likely' to be second-hottest year on record: EU monitor

alsoReported.title: Cop31 will expose the conflicts and contradictions of the world's fossil fuel reliance
COP31 summit faces tough test as climate threats mount

article: The EU's Copernicus climate service says October 2026 was the warmest October on record, 1.75C above the average before industrialisation, and the third month in a row above 1.5C[^21]. It says 2026 will most likely be the second-hottest year, with a 20% chance it ties or beats 2024[^21]. A very strong El Niño, a natural warming of the Pacific that heats the whole planet for a while, has not yet peaked and could make 2027 the hottest year yet[^21].

COP31, the yearly UN climate summit, runs from November 9 to 20 in Antalya, with nearly 200 countries and more than 100,000 people expected[^23]. It has an unusual split: Australia runs the negotiations and Turkey runs the programme of voluntary pledges[^22]. The US government is not taking part in the negotiations, although a congressional delegation will attend[^23].

Key arguments will be about money and energy. African negotiators want a pledge to triple funding for adaptation, meaning help coping with heat, floods and drought[^23]. A proposed goal would have electricity supply 35% of the world's final energy use by 2035; the COP31 president says "electrification is the answer"[^23][^22]. The Guardian notes coal is still Turkey's biggest power source[^22].

Expectations are modest. A former French chief negotiator told AFP "this is not going to be the COP that changes the world"[^23]. My read: high oil prices from the Iran war cut both ways, making clean power more attractive while pushing some countries to secure fossil fuel supplies.

question.text: Many towns voted this week to block new AI data centres near them. If more places do the same, what might happen next: where would the data centres go instead, who would gain or lose, and what would change for people who use AI?
